chunks: "Galvanic isolation means two parts of a circuit have no direct electrical connection: no conductive path for DC current. They can't share a wire or a ground.
But information or energy can still cross, by some other physical means.
The classic ways are light, as in an optocoupler; a magnetic field, as in a transformer or a coil on a chip; or an electric field through a capacitor, as in a capacitive digital isolator.
The word comes from Galvani, from the idea of galvanic current, meaning current through a conductor.

What it buys you is that the two sides can sit at completely different voltages: a microcontroller on one side and a 400 volt DC bus or mains on the other, with a high-voltage withstand rating on the barrier.
It breaks ground loops, blocks DC and low-frequency common-mode, and keeps a fault on one side from reaching the other. But it's not perfect.

The barrier has capacitance, about a picofarad for a signal isolator and tens of picofarads for a power transformer, so fast common-mode transients still push current across, which is why common-mode transient immunity matters.
It has a finite voltage rating, a working voltage and a withstand voltage.
And each side still needs its own supply and reference; isolating the signal isn't enough if the power isn't isolated too."
